comments.author: @PierreH1968
comments.text:
The missing link that causes a slowdown in AI Models intelligence is the lack of quality training sets originating in human environments. Lack of stereovision and scale causes glitches in recreation of visual artifacts (6 fingers humans, facial morphism for the same character...) Also, it lacks physical interaction and true daily intellectual communication in a physical context. It is something that will only be improved through the introduction of robots in human environments or training with advanced synthetic data (with caution).
Another challenge lies in the Question-answer format. The model forms an answer solely based on the question. Few models ask precisions about missing axioms or ambiguity in the questioning hindering the reinforcement learning quality).

comments.author: @Corbald
comments.text:
(just a bunch of thoughts:)

Imagine you invented the welder. Your first iteration could only get so hot, but your friends were impressed, anyway. Eventually, you got it to the point it could weld steel. People were still impressed, but less so than before, because they'd seen your rate of progress slow down over time, because solving the most fundamental problems came first, and iteration for the sake of efficiency and ergonomics came last. Then you release it, and it makes a big splash, but people are saying that you've hit a wall, because the welder can't get much better than it is.


Here's the thing, you've just invented a tool for which an entire civilization will now find applications, from building construction to the world's largest ships, and suddenly democratize the ability to join two pieces of metal in a permanent bond, a skill previously held only by blacksmiths and riveters.

Now imagine that welder can design the next, better welder.

I admit the analogy is a bit stretched, but you get the idea.

Even if they've hit a wall with training data, there's still a lot of avenues which are now much, much more effective at scaling the system, because the system's previous scaling enabled them. From post-training architectures, such as Chain of Thought to real-time re-training on acquired data, from combining different architectures like Reinforcement Learning with Large Language models, to exploring the very concepts of Latent Spaces (structure/search/etc...), what we have now, with GPT-o1, is more than sufficient to fuel decades of breakthroughs.

But they haven't. I still haven't seen a convincing argument, with actual sources, or charts, or any evidence at all, that major companies like OpenAI, Google, Meta, etc.. are actually having any trouble with any such wall, and each model I've seen released so far has blown the last entirely out of the water.

Anyone play AI Dungeon in 2019 when it came out? Have you tried it recently?

Hell, I'd kill for the "Token cost so low it's not worth tracking" (or whatever Sam said.) Give the public that, with faster inference, and watch us figure out AGI without more training scaling, because all it really needs now is the capacity to second-guess it's self. Put 100 GPT-01s in a room for 100 simulated hours of recursive inference, and see if there's a problem known to man that they can't solve. Now do that for every interaction. OpenAI has barely scratched the surface with 'o1 and post-training architecture.

I'm 44. What's happening now is exactly the same as what happened with the Internet, which I predate, and cell-phones, which I watched grow up. Neither of those is really slowing down, or threatening to stop innovating, and the only difference between them and AI, is AI is hyper-exponential. Even if it does slow down (and it won't, mark my words), merely exponential growth is still as good as we've ever done before.

comments.text:
The problem with this new Turing test is that it is static. Given it to a group of AI developers, does not prevent the developers from tuning the AI model to this type of problem.  A more effective test might be to have a series of tests to which the AI model has not been exposed. Have it produce its results to a collection of the tests and measure its success. Very the contents of the test material, to eliminate repeated test learning. 

I recall IBM's appearance on Jeopardy. Watson was very good at answering "factual" questions (e.g. who is buried in Grants tomb). But it did not answer a simple reasoning question. What key on a keyboard is simpler to a woman's dress style. The answer was the letter "A". Of course, after the developers heard this question, it was simple to add that question and answer to the training data.
